text: Chapter 17, nearby friends. Let's see how locations get pushed in real time.

A shop never moves, but a friend keeps walking. So we can't scan the whole database on every refresh. Instead, each online device reports its location every thirty seconds. With ten million people online, that's about three hundred thirty-four thousand updates per second.

The phone and the server stay connected over a WebSocket. It opens once and stays open, so the device can report, and the server can push at any moment. Letting phones talk to each other directly isn't practical. Mobile networks are flaky, and it drains the battery. So the backend relays everything.

The relay is built on Redis Pub/Sub. Every user gets their own channel. The servers that hold A's friends subscribe to A's channel. When A reports a location, it's published to that channel, and every subscriber receives it at once.

Here's the full path of one update. The location arrives at a WebSocket server. It's written to the history database, the location cache is updated, and then it's published to the user's own channel. Redis broadcasts it to the subscribers: the servers holding A's friends.

Each receiving server has one last step: compute the distance. If the friend is within five miles, push it to the client. Otherwise, drop it. With four hundred friends per person and ten percent online, one update fans out to about forty.

The location cache holds only the latest position: user ID, latitude, longitude, and a timestamp, with a TTL. If a user stops reporting, the entry expires, which means they're offline. History goes to Cassandra separately, and never touches the nearby-friends read path.

Why Pub/Sub? Because it's light. A channel with no subscribers keeps no messages, unlike a message queue. Channel names can be agreed in advance, so nobody coordinates when a user comes online. And losing an occasional point is fine, because the next one arrives thirty seconds later.

The real bottleneck is throughput. Three hundred thirty-four thousand updates, each fanned out forty times, is about fourteen million pushes per second. Channel memory is around two hundred gigabytes, so two hundred-gigabyte Redis servers are enough. But at one hundred thousand per second per machine, we need at least one hundred forty.

So we shard the channels across a Redis cluster. ZooKeeper or etcd records which nodes are alive and where channels live. A WebSocket server uses that to find the node for a channel, then publishes or subscribes there. We shard with consistent hashing.

Channels carry subscription state, so you can't add or remove nodes freely like stateless servers. When a channel moves, its subscribers must resubscribe, and a few points may be lost. That's acceptable here, but do it at low traffic. Consistent hashing keeps the moves to a minimum.
Remember three ideas: long-lived connections, one channel per user, and distance filtering. At scale, shard the channels.
